name: Everpix
epitaph: Loved by its users. Outrun by 'free'.
oneLiner: A paid app that gathered all your photos from your phone, computer and social media in one place and automatically picked the best ones.
causeOfDeath: Users loved it and many paid, but money ran out before it could grow; investors doubted photo apps, and Google and Apple offered similar tools free.
moneyNote: From Everpix's own published financials: four rounds totalling about $2.3M (notes in 2011 and 2013, a $1M seed in 2012 at $7.8M post-money). It shut down with no sale.
inOneMinute: Everpix **automatically organised all your photos** and showed you the best ones. Of 50,000 people who signed up, **7,000 paid** for it.
But it made $40,000 a month, which **covered running costs, not the team's salaries**. It needed a bigger round, and investors kept saying no.
Google and Apple were adding similar features for free. Everpix shut in late 2013, then **published all its data** so others could learn.
killerLine: **A great product is not a plan.** Know how you'll reach users and how long your money lasts before you need investors to say yes.

chapters.title: The idea: fix the photo mess
chapters.body: By 2011, phones had turned everyone into a photographer. Thousands of pictures sat scattered across phones, laptops, Facebook and Flickr. Pierre-Olivier Latour, who had worked at Apple, called it the 'photo mess'. In late spring 2011 he started building Everpix, and was soon joined by Kevin Quennesson, also ex-Apple, and designer Wayne Fan. Everpix pulled **all your photos into one place** in the cloud (online storage), removed near-duplicates and picked out highlights, so you could relive your best moments without scrolling through junk. It was a finalist at TechCrunch Disrupt in September 2011. Think of it as a better, smarter photo gallery app, long before Google Photos.

chapters.title: The rise: a product people paid for
chapters.body: Everpix raised small amounts carefully: $800,000 in notes in 2011, then a **$1 million seed round in July 2012** led by Index Ventures, at a $7.8 million valuation. It opened for business in September 2012 at $4.99 a month or about $40 a year. Unlike many apps, it asked people to pay, and they did. Its co-founder said its paid conversion rates were significantly higher than typical for free-to-paid apps. By the end, **50,000 people had signed up and 7,000 were paying**, with 400 million photos imported. The team kept shipping new features almost monthly: similar-photo detection, highlights, daily 'flashback' emails, and apps for iPhone, Windows and Android.

chapters.title: The cracks: investors say no
chapters.body: To grow, Everpix needed a Series A (a bigger round of funding, usually millions of dollars). In early 2013 it went on its first tour of venture capitalists. They passed. Some doubted anyone could make **real money from online photos**. Others said distribution, getting the app in front of millions of people, was too tough, and that photos were a noisy, crowded category. In April 2013 Everpix took a $525,000 bridge loan to keep going. Then, in May and June 2013, Google and Apple both showed **free tools that organised photos automatically**. Flickr was offering a free terabyte of storage. Second and third investor tours that summer also failed.

chapters.title: The fall: covering costs, but not salaries
chapters.body: By late 2013, subscriptions brought in about **$40,000 a month**. That covered variable costs (storage and servers that grow with users) but not fixed costs like salaries and rent. Over its life, Everpix earned about $281,000 and spent about $2.67 million, most of it on its team. With no Series A, on 5 November 2013 the founders announced Everpix would shut down. They worked with a reporter from The Verge on the story of their final weeks. Then they did something rare: they **published their metrics, investor feedback and finances on GitHub**, so other founders could learn from their failure. In May 2015, Google launched Google Photos with free unlimited storage.

charts.title: Lifetime money in vs money out
charts.takeaway: Users really paid, but income was about a tenth of what the company spent.

charts.title: Where the money went
charts.takeaway: People were by far the biggest cost; servers came second.

mistakes.title: Bet survival on one big round
mistakes.explain: Everpix's plan needed a **Series A to cover salaries**. When three investor tours failed, there was no plan B. Revenue covered server costs but not the team. A smaller team, or a plan to reach break-even on its own, could have bought time to keep growing.

mistakes.title: Built features faster than it built reach
mistakes.explain: The team launched a new feature almost every month and wrote over 200,000 lines of code. But investors' biggest worry was **distribution**: getting the app to millions of people. A brilliant product that too few people discover can't grow fast enough to impress investors.

mistakes.title: Competed head-on with free giants
mistakes.explain: In 2013, **Google and Apple announced free tools** that organised photos automatically, and Flickr gave away a terabyte of storage. Everpix was better, but asking people to pay for something big companies give free is a very hard sell. Big platforms can afford to lose money on photos because it keeps people inside their phones and services.

mistakes.title: Picked a category investors feared
mistakes.explain: VCs told Everpix that online photos had historically been **hard to make money from** and called it a crowded category. Founders can prove investors wrong, but they need extra runway to do it, which Everpix didn't have. Even strong paying users could not change that view in time.

warningSigns: Does your company die if your next funding round doesn't happen?
Are Google, Apple or another giant offering something similar to your product for free?
Have investors repeatedly said 'great product, but how will you get users?'
Are you shipping new features every month while sign-ups stay flat?
Do your monthly earnings cover servers but not salaries, with no date when that changes?

lessons.title: Build a path to 'ramen profitable'
lessons.detail: Work out the revenue that covers your whole team's basic costs, not just servers. Plan to hit it before you need a big round, even if that means a smaller team for longer.

lessons.title: Distribution is part of the product
lessons.detail: From the start, decide how users will find you: partnerships, referrals, SEO, a community. Spend as much thought on that as on features.

lessons.title: Expect giants to give your feature away
lessons.detail: If your product lives inside phones Google or Apple make, assume they may offer a free version. Build something they won't, like a specific niche or a service layer.

lessons.title: Paying users are a real signal
lessons.detail: 7,000 paying subscribers is meaningful. Everpix proved willingness to pay. If you have that, consider growing slowly and profitably instead of waiting for a VC to bless it.

lessons.title: Share what you learn
lessons.detail: Everpix published its numbers, VC feedback and finances so others could learn. Writing an honest post-mortem helps you, your team and the next founder, and builds respect.

quote.text: we didn't succeed in raising our Series A in the highly competitive VC funding market.
quote.context: From the post-mortem they published on GitHub after shutting down, 2013

afterlife.text: The founders published hundreds of files on GitHub: metrics, monthly investor reports, their pitch deck, unedited feedback from investors who passed, and full financials. It became one of the most honest startup post-mortems ever shared. Eighteen months later, Google launched Google Photos with free unlimited storage, reaching 100 million users in five months. The problem Everpix chose to solve was real; the market went to the companies that could afford to give it away.

disputed.claim: Everpix was 'the world's best photo startup'
disputed.note: This was The Verge's framing in its 2013 story; it is a matter of opinion, so the page sticks to the published numbers.
The founders did not publish a monthly burn figure; spreading the lifetime loss over 26 months gives roughly $92,000 a month, but that is our estimate, not theirs.
